speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Before 2016, it was not mandatory to appoint a private trustee to administer bankruptcy cases as the trustee in bankruptcy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: As part of the Ministry of Law (MinLaw)'s ongoing review of the bankruptcy administration regime in Singapore, in 2016, the Government introduced two key initiatives.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, a requirement for Institutional Creditors (ICs) making bankruptcy applications to apply for Private Trustees in Bankruptcy, which I will call PTIBs, to be appointed as the trustee administering the bankruptcy, instead of the OA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Second, a Differentiated Discharge Framework (DDF) was introduced.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This serves to streamline work processes, and also creates a more rehabilitative discharge process with clear time frames and conditions for bankrupts to be discharged.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: To support the shift towards a fully PTIB-administered bankruptcy regime, the Bill introduces an amendment to improve operational flexibility in determining PTIBs' remuneration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Private debt recovery lies at the heart of bankruptcy administration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Bankruptcy typically involves the creditor seeking redress for non-payment of a debt, or a debtor seeking relief from overwhelming debts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A PTIB-administered bankruptcy regime aims to reduce the usage of public resources involved in private debt recovery, whilst ensuring that bankruptcy cases in Singapore continue to be managed in an orderly manner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For instance, in jurisdictions like the United States and Canada, the law mandates the appointment of the equivalent of PTIBs for every bankruptcy case in those jurisdictions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 2 of the Bill, therefore, amends sections 36(1) and (2) of the Insolvency, Restructuring and.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Dissolution Act (IRDA): (a) to mandate the appointment of PTIBs to act as trustees in all bankruptcy cases; and (b) save for cases where the OA consents to be appointed as the trustee in bankruptcy.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Moving forward, the OA will provide consent only in cases where the OA considers them to be in the public interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Typically, they will include cases where public finances are affected, such as, for instance, cases involving the misuse of public funds or where there are debts owed to the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These are not meant to be exhaustive illustrations.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: However, I will add that this does not mean that the OA will consent to act as the trustee in every case where there might be elements of public interest.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The OA will continue to retain the discretion on whether to take up these cases and the OA will consider whether the public interest element is sufficiently compelling vis-à-vis other considerations, giving the appropriate weight to each of these factors before deciding whether to give such consent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With this new regime, the OA will take on a more regulatory role to ensure the PTIBs' competencies and legislative compliance in bankruptcy administration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Statutory duties, such as the powers of investigation, as well as that of prosecution, will continue to reside with the OA.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We have assessed, at present, that there is sufficient capacity in the PTIB industry to take on the additional cases following these changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In other words, we made an assessment as to what the likely case load will be after these changes.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: We looked at the amount of resources in the industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In our assessment, there is sufficient capacity in the PTIB industry.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: My Ministry has engaged industry stakeholders on these proposals.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The stakeholders include insolvency practitioners who are eligible to handle, but are not yet currently handling, bankruptcy administration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: MinLaw will continue to engage the industry to keep them abreast of the developments and provide the necessary support that may be required for them to take on this role.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Currently, section 41(1) of the IRDA states that a trustee's remuneration must be approved in the following manner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, by agreement between the trustees and the creditors' committee.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: If there is no such agreement, or if there is no creditors' committee, remuneration has to be determined by a special resolution of creditors at a meeting convened by the trustee.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Where there is no determination under either of the previous two modes, then the Court has to determine the PTIBs' remuneration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In our consultation with industry players, they have pointed out that they face obstacles in forming a creditors' committee for many cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This includes unsuccessful attempts at convening a creditors' meeting to vote on a trustee's remuneration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: There is also a lack of response from creditors in some cases.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Those were the feedback that we received from industry players.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This has resulted in extra costs being incurred in bankruptcy administration as the PTIBs will have to appoint solicitors to apply to Court to approve their remuneration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This, in turn, reduces the amount left available for distribution to creditors as costs and expenses of administration are given priority in the distribution of a bankrupt's property.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Therefore, Sir, to simplify the process for determining PTIBs' remuneration and to keep the costs of bankruptcy administration low, clause 3 amends section 41(1) and inserts new subsections (1)(b)(ii) and (4) to provide for an additional means of determining PTIB's remuneration via agreement between the PTIB and all the creditors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The creditors will be deemed to have agreed if they have not objected to the remuneration sought by the PTIB in the prescribed manner and within the prescribed time.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: I would stress that the creditors' rights to object to such renumeration will be preserved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And if indeed the creditors do object, the PTIBs will still have to secure either a special resolution at a creditors' meeting or they will have to go to Court for approval.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These amendments will help PTIBs' fees remain affordable by keeping the costs down, even as they take on more cases and also seek to improve returns for creditors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: First, the enhancement of protection of persons dealing with bankrupts in commercial transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Apart from amendments that allow changes to the current bankruptcy regime, this Bill will also introduce measures to better protect persons dealing with bankrupts in commercial transactions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These amendments address concerns where members of the public were not aware that they were dealing with a bankrupt person, especially when large sums of money are involved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These measures will be introduced via two amendments.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This will complement existing subsection 1(a), which makes it an offence for a bankrupt to obtain credit without first disclosing his bankruptcy status.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: For this amendment, what do we mean by the taking of a deposit?

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the amendment, when we say "deposit", it refers to an advance payment for the supply of goods or services.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This can be in the form of money or other in-kind consideration.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: A bankrupt who is an employee of a renovation company collects a deposit of $10,000 from a customer who has engaged the company to perform renovation works.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The bankrupt in this case will have to disclose his bankruptcy status at the time he receives the $10,000, even though he might have been authorised by the company to collect deposits.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Clause 10 also includes language which makes it immaterial whether the individual receives the deposit in his or her own account or on the account of another person.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: So, in the context of my example, the employee receiving it on the account of the company will also be obliged to make this disclosure.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: It is also immaterial whether the deposit is received as full or partial payment.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Hence, clause 10 also provides that the Minister for Law may exempt any person or class of persons from this new offence by order in the Gazette.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This allows the public to conduct better due diligence when transacting with persons who are undischarged bankrupts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Such information will be available along with other such existing information in the register of bankrupts that is already publicly searchable upon the payment of a prescribed search fee.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These two amendments will also apply and be in force against bankrupts whose bankruptcy orders were made under the repealed Bankruptcy Act by way of clause 12 of the Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: And the final set deals with amendments which seek to extend the validity period of the SIP for an additional two years, to 28 January 2026.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: This was part of the Government's response to COVID-19 and comprised temporary insolvency processes which help eligible MSCs by restructuring the debts of viable companies to rehabilitate the business, or in some cases to wind up the company where the business has ceased to be viable.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These processes are meant to be simpler, faster and low-cost in nature to optimise resources and potentially maximise returns to creditors.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: Under the normal compulsory liquidation processes, the average time taken to complete the liquidation of such a company would be roughly three to four years.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In comparison, liquidations under the SIP have been completed within an average of six months from the date the case has been accepted into the SIP.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: The validity period of the SIP lasts for only three years presently.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: These amendments will allow my Ministry to provide continued support for such MSCs which may face operational challenges, particularly in the context of the current economic environment of rising inflation and interest rates.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: In the meantime, I would add that my Ministry is also reviewing the SIP with the view to making certain features permanent.

speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
text: With that, Mr Speaker, I beg to move.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In my speech, I will focus on one of the aims that the hon Minister articulated, that is, to mandate the appointment of PTIBs in, generally, all bankruptcy cases.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The key motivation behind this aim is to provide a more efficient use of the Public Service by focusing on the regulatory role of the Government and decanting non-regulatory service functions to the private sector.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I see this proposal as the final move in an orderly transformation of insolvency and bankruptcy processes that commenced in 2016.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The hon Minister has already mentioned it in his speech and I need only mention two milestones.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: First, for corporate insolvencies, the Official Receiver has already stopped being the liquidator of last resort.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In his place, private liquidators are appointed by the Court.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect to bankruptcy applications by ICs, such as retail banks, ICs are required to apply for PTIBs to be appointed to administer the bankruptcy, instead of the OA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Through this, we will be able to gain the full extent of the efficiencies by redeploying resources under the Insolvency and Public Trustee's Office to perform regulatory functions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In essence, we are placing the core of the Government's function within the Civil Service while allow the private sector to take care of some of its service functions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For this system to work, however, we must be sure that the private sector has the capacity to provide such a function at a high level of competency and at affordable cost.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This means that we need to ensure a strong supply of licensed insolvency practitioners who would be willing to undertake such assignments for fees that are not prohibitive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Both outcomes, of course, can come about purely as a result of the operations of the free market.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is where we need to be mindful about the market conditions and take the necessary steps to strike a proper balance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On one hand, there should be sufficient commercial incentives to ensure that there is a ready pool of practitioners to tap on for such work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: On the other hand, we need to ensure that costs are kept reasonable and the statutory objectives under the IRDA, particularly that those in relation to the investigation of the bankrupt's affairs are met.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, there are several firms providing PTIB services for ICs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The provision of this sum itself is mandated under the Insolvency, Restructuring and Dissolution (Official Assignee's Fees) Regulation 2020.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The idea is to work within the deposit amount.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To make the model financially sustainable, the PTIBs engage in what can be described as a volume game.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: By agreeing to working within the deposit amount, the practitioners can be assured of a significant volume of cases from the ICs for which the practitioners may be appointed as PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They can also benefit from being assigned cases which are referred to as "meaty" cases, where there is a good prospect for PTIBs to recover substantial assets and monies that form part of the estate of the bankrupt for distribution to creditors and get their costs to be paid from, as a matter of priority from the estate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For non-ICs, I believe the considerations will be materially different.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They cannot promise large volumes like institutions, such as retail banks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: How can we then ensure that the costs of petitioning creditors who are non-ICs are kept reasonable by reason of the privatisation move?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One group of people I am particularly concerned about are debtors who have just cause to apply for bankruptcy to avail themselves of the protection of bankruptcy laws.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They may be put in a more difficult position.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: These debtors who apply to be bankrupts, by definition, do not have much money.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, under IRDA, only creditors are allowed to apply for a practitioner to be appointed as PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Should the market move against them such that they are required to pay more than the current sum of $1,850 for the appointment of PTIBs, this may stymie the debtors' efforts to get the protection of the bankruptcy laws.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Next, I would be grateful for the hon Minister's clarification on the circumstances in which the OA is expected to administer the estate of the bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In clause 2 of the amendment Bill, it is provided that the OA may consent to be the trustee of the bankrupt's estate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I did not see any elaboration on the circumstances in which the OA may give consent in the explanatory statement to the Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I am glad to note the hon Minister's point, that the OA is expected to give his consent in cases of public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I have in mind situations where petitioning creditors or debtors cannot get practitioners to be appointed as PTIBs, despite their best efforts or having regard to their specific financial circumstances.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This question is related to my earlier point on the possible financial hardship on the debtor.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If the difficulty relates to debtors facing financial hardship and being unable to pay for the PTIBs, what will be their recourse?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Another area that I seek clarification on is the OA's role where the office of the PTIB becomes vacant, be it as a result of resignation, death and so on.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: To my understanding, the OA will have to step in to take over as trustee until the vacancy is filled.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This provision that requires this – section 45 of the IRDA	– is unaffected by the amendment Bill.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Having regard to the objective of this Bill, which is for the OA to exit the arena of administration of a bankrupt's estate, save when it is in public's interest, may I please ask how it is proposed that the OA will deal with such situations?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One final area which I want to touch on before moving to my next point concerns aligning the commercial interests of PTIBs with the aims under IRDA in relation to the administration of the bankrupt's affairs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a general caveat when using the private sector as a partner to provide public services.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While the incentive of the public sector is to safeguard the public interest, the private sector has no such incentive.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: PTIBs are not, prima facie, remunerated on the basis of the efforts expended to check the conduct and the affairs of the bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Instead, we must ensure that there are rules and incentives in place to ensure that the commercial interests of the PTIBs are motivated to align with the demands of public interest.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: For example, we could require specific audits and checks to be conducted on PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I now turn to the part of the Bill that introduces measures to make it more efficient for PTIBs to conduct their work.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This resolves a big problem in practice, because creditors often tend not to revert timeously on such issues, making it difficult for PTIBs to be paid.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: With respect to what is meant by "prescribed manner", I take it that it is intended to be provided in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I suggest that the hon Minister consider prescribing that notices on remuneration may be sent by emails too.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This will increase efficiency and reduce disbursements, especially when we have cases involving numerous creditors.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I also note that in the format of proofs of debt that creditors are supposed to file, contact details, such as email addresses are already supposed to be provided.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hence, PTIBs should be able to use this information for notification purposes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The OA may allow any person who needs access to such details, which conceivably will include a PTIB, for the purposes of administering the bankrupt's estate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a good move and I support it.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The question that arises is what other information that a PTIB may reasonably need for the proper and efficient administration of the bankrupt's estate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: One possible area is the registered address of the bankrupt which can obviously change over time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Currently, under section 399(2) of IRDA, a bankrupt is deemed to have informed the OA of the change of his registered address when he makes a report of the change under section 10 of the National Registration Act 1965 (NRA).

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a deeming provision in section 399(3) of the IRDA which deems service of notice at the registered address as conclusive evidence of the fact of service.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I may be wrong, but it seems to me that the OA has ready access to the database of registered addresses under the NRA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If I am right, I should point out that PTIBs may not be in a similar position as the OAs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I wonder if, instead of maintaining a definitive list of information that the OA can allow inspection of it would be better to provide that the list may be expanded to contain information that the hon Minister, in his discretion, may prescribe through subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In this way, the information that PTIBs need can be provided much faster, which will, in turn, allow for more efficiency and cost reduction.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Such information can include the new registered address of the debtor or any other information that may be relevant for the administration of the bankrupt's estate.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This information can include names and contact details of related persons for PTIBs to investigate cases of unfair preferences and transactions at undervalue, something that the hon Minister is very well aware of since he was a well-noted lawyer dealing with insolvency work before he joined the front bench.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: All the above are minutiae in themselves but added together, these little drops make a mighty sea.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They make the administration of the insolvency process leaner, simpler and less costly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As a while, they ensure that the PTIB can go about with their duties efficiently, which will in turn allow their fees to be kept as low as possible.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If this cannot be done now, perhaps this is a suggestion that can be explored in the future.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They shared with me their experience liaising with the OA officers for various purposes, ranging from proposing instalment payments of their debts to obtaining permission to leave the country.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While they had no complaint about the way they were treated, a common dissatisfaction was the perceived difficulty in contacting the officers or delays in obtaining responses.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This was an issue I first raised a decade ago during MinLaw's Committee of Supply (COS) debates.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Since then, I have noted the Ministry's constructive moves to improve the situation, including taking steps to rationalise the OAs workload.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This scheme for institutional creditors to appoint PTIBs would have significantly reduced the number of new bankruptcies under the OAs direct management since institutional creditors accounted for more than 50% of bankruptcy applications.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to MinLaw's register of insolvency practitioners, today, there are 187 lawyers and accountants registered as potential PTIBs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Debtors, too, who wish to voluntarily apply for bankruptcy who also have to appoint a PTIB.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It should fall to the creditor and the debtor to bear the cost of bankruptcy administration.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, I have some queries on evaluating our experience with the PTIB scheme thus far and one query on the Bill itself.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Five years ago, Singapore commenced the use of PTIBs in bankruptcy cases involving institutional creditors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Now that the Bill proposes to extend the use of PTIBs to non-institutional creditors and voluntary bankruptcies as well, it is appropriate to ask what can be learned from the past five years.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Have there been better outcomes in bankruptcies, not just in terms of freeing up public resources but also better experiences for creditors and debtors?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While no formal action has been taken, it would be good for the Ministry to elaborate on how the OA has exercised its supervisory role over the PTIBs under section 42 of the Act.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, has the OA had to inquire into any complaints by creditors or debtors and if so, what was the nature of those complaints?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Specifically, from the debtors' perspective, I would like to highlight three aspects which I think are important in assessing whether the PTIB system is working optimally.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Bankruptcy cases are now being handled not by a public officer from the OA's office, but by a PTIB chosen by the creditor whose fees are also underwritten by the creditor.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is sometimes said that he who pays the piper calls the tune.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Have there been any complaints from debtors that the PTIBs have been unfair to them?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A second aspect concerns the fees to be paid to PTIBs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: From my reading, the fees are not fixed according to a scale but are decided by the creditors in each case.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Is there a wide variation in the rates of fees charged?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If the range is too wide, this is not desirable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have also heard Mr Murali's concerns earlier on the possible financial hardship that might be caused if high fees are charged moving forward on non-institutional creditors and debtors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This was a common grouse of bankrupts in the past.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Have PTIBs be able to respond efficiently to debtors' communications and requests?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I also have a query on clause 2 regarding the proposed expansion of the PTIB scheme to non-institutional creditors and voluntary bankruptcies.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Given that non-institutional creditors and debtors may not have knowledge and experience in insolvency matters, how will they decide which insolvency practitioner to propose as their PTIB?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will more resources be put up to assist them in making the selection of insolvency practitioner?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We know that bankrupt persons end up in bankruptcy for a myriad of reasons, including misfortune, bad timing and being guarantors for the debts of others.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Bankruptcy can be debilitating and disempowering, as bankrupts are stigmatised and disqualified from public office and various professions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I do hope that as we move toward a system of having PTIBs as the default, the bankruptcy experience can be a less painful one.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have three points of clarification on the Bill.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: While the debts between individuals and their creditors are private matters, we do have a public interest in a well-functioning bankruptcy system as part of our economy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: MinLaw has stated that the OA will be taking on a regulatory role over private trustees.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: What standards will the OA apply when reviewing their performance?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Minister clarify the roles of the OA and the Court in supervising trustees?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Ultimately, in that case, the Court took a view that it would only intervene if the trustee had acted so perversely that no reasonable trustee would have done so.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: If the OA gives similar deference in exercising its supervisory role, creditors and debtors might find it hard to hold trustees accountable if they disagree with the trustee's decision.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can Minister clarify how creditors or debtors can raise complaints against the private trustee?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Should they look to the OA or to the Courts?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My second clarification relates to accessibility to the bankruptcy process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: For example, if the estate is too small relative to the trustee's fees to be practical, or if there are too few practitioners available.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Will the OA step in to act itself in these cases?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Does the Ministry consider there to be enough licensed practitioners to meet the needs of the market?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: With cryptocurrency, we saw rapid growth and speculation in new asset classes spanning multiple jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How will we ensure that trustees can properly manage and distribute digital or other new types of assets?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications, Sir, I stand in support of the Bill.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I am a dispute lawyer in a law firm with an insolvency practice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The proposed amendments in this Bill will help save public resources and make better use of the OA's involvement in bankruptcy proceedings.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I also welcome the Ministry's calibrated approach by proposing these amendments after the learning experiences drawn from the earlier initiatives introduced in 2016, which required institutional creditors to appoint PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, on the recourse or redress against errant PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Third, protection of members of the public from certain transactions with undischarged bankrupts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I understand that to date, the administration of bankruptcy cases filed by ICs have been smooth and that there has been no action taken against PTIBs by the Court or the OA.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, while there are no actions taken, may I ask if there has been any complaints or investigations against PTIBs during this period?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: And if so, how many cases have there been since 2017?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The role and oversight of PTIBs will be more important now.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I hope that this will allay concerns of individual creditors or laypersons who may not have the means to hire PTIBs, from not proceeding with a petition for bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Given the expanded appointment of PTIBs now for all bankruptcy cases, would this overlap with the work done by debt recovery firms or credit counselling firms in the market?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Would more creditors or debtors now go directly to these firms instead of undergoing the bankruptcy regime in the Courts?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I appreciate that the Ministry has consulted stakeholders and I appreciate that the Ministry will continue to consult along the way.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In this regard, we can still learn from some of the lessons and experience from other jurisdictions abroad.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In the United States (US), given the high volume of bankruptcy cases and increasing quantum of debt in total, the US General Accounting Office warned that there is a high risk of private trustee fraud if there is no rigorous review of trustee candidates, no proper conflict-of-interest declaration, no enhanced reporting requirements and no sufficient funding for oversight by the Department of Justice (DOJ).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Canada, their Licensed Insolvency Trustee (LIT) must have the requisite knowledge, experience and skills to be granted a licence from the Office of the Superintendent of Bankruptcy (OSB).

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: LITs are subject to ongoing oversight by the OSB and must adhere to federal standards of practice, including the Code of Ethics for Trustees.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Hence, with the expanded regime proposed in this Bill, would similar standards or codes for PTIBs be implemented or updated in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Besides overseeing and regulating PTIBs, what are the plans by MinLaw or the OA to ensure the standards and quality of our PTIBs in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, would there be continuous training or mandatory courses for PTIBs?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Separately, here, there is no solicitor-client privilege between a trustee and a debtor currently.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, in Canada, the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act and the Canadian Association of Insolvency and Restructuring Professionals rules prohibit a trustee from disclosing confidential information to the public unless required by law or with the debtor's permission.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If I may ask the hon Minister, would there be a similar rule of confidentiality here?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What are the obligations owed by the PTIB and the debtor, perhaps with the overriding obligation or duty owed by PTIBs to the Court and the OA.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: With regard to PTIBs' remuneration, I agree with the additional means of determining such remuneration.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For instance, there is a deemed consent for remuneration if no objection is received from creditors within a stipulated period of time.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, what are the safeguards to ensure that such notice is appropriately given, especially for individual or layperson creditors?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I echo the hon Member Murali Pillai's suggestion to include emails as a mode of transmission for such notice.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Separately, there can be more regulation or transparency in terms of remuneration.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In Canada, LITs do not typically charge for their first consultation and the remuneration is regulated by the federal government.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The last part of my speech is on the protection of public members.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, what is the rationale behind the quantum of $10,000?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: What if there is a series of transactions with multiple persons with an aggregate amounting to at least $10,000?

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If the undischarged bankrupt takes in several deposits from various people totalling more than $10,000, then for the protection of the greater public, it would make sense for the entire series of transactions to be taken into consideration for the issue of non-disclosure and not just base on the quantum of one single transaction alone.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is most welcomed as it enhances the due diligence when transacting with persons who are undischarged bankrupts.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Currently, to do so would require a Court litigation search and this would involve costs, which may be prohibitive for some.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The process itself may be too tedious or unknown to laypersons.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Borrowing the words used by the President of our Law Society, Mr Adrian Tan, this morning and I may paraphrase a bit, "Justice is not the privilege of a few but a promise made to everyone".

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is our calling for those of us in the legal profession.

speaker: Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Notwithstanding my clarifications, I stand in support of this Bill.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On the one hand, it tries to protect creditors by ensuring that the assets of a bankrupt can be properly accounted for, realised and distributed in a fair way to all creditors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This prevents creditors from feeling pressurised to act unilaterally or to act faster than the others.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Counterintuitively, it also protects the interests of the bankrupts themselves by taking away the stress and pressure of having to deal with a larger number of creditors and allows them to continue working, earning a salary and meeting their basic living requirements while ensuring that contributions are also made towards the payment of their debts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In facilitating the administration of a bankruptcy, it is usually helpful to have a professional – often, it is an accountant	– involved as this will ensure an orderly realisation and distribution of the assets of the bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The professional should be disinterested and act impartially as between the debtor and the creditors.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Where a professional is not appointed, the default would be for the OA to administer the estate of the bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This would be, I believe, especially the case where the assets of the estate are small and the debts are small.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This has, naturally, resulted in a heavy case load for the OA's office as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This will have the dual benefits of having a professional administering all bankruptcies, by the sound of it, except for the few where public interest is triggered, while at the same time reducing the burden on the OA.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The only concern I have with this proposal is whether it would mean that those with smaller claims and estates would no longer be able to avail themselves of the protections afforded by bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If we take the classic example of a small estate – a person without any substantial assets – the estate itself may still take some time to administer, so there is a risk that the professional who is doing this will be liable for the costs in the meantime.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There are also considerable benefits for a person with a small amount of debt to be provided the protections offered by bankruptcy, such as the moratoriums against actions and avoiding the stress of having multiple creditors following him.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: His creditors will also be protected by knowing that they will be dealt with equitably rather than each one feeling pressurised to take their own enforcement action if the bankruptcy is deemed to be uneconomic.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They would then be at risk of dealing with someone who is in substance insolvent but may not have been made a bankrupt because there was no PTIB found who was able to act.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This problem may be particularly acute for those who have, for example, gone into a cycle of debt starting with consumer credit, taking on more credit, say, from licensed money lenders at high interest rates to pay off earlier debts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Ms Sylvia Lim, Mr Louis Ng, Mr Zhulkarnain Abdul Rahim and Mr Vikram Nair, I believe, asked how we can ensure accessibility to PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Ms Lim herself, from her research, found 187 licensed insolvency practitioners.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in other words, out of the 187, 183 of them are qualified to take on this role as PTIB, but only about a third of them are currently taking it up; obviously, under the older regime, where only ICs appoint PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in other words, there is headroom for this to grow into that space.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Should there be a need to review these numbers, we will do so.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Debtors and creditors will be able to use information that is on the list to discuss with PTIBs about the appropriateness of taking up their cases and which PTIB they might want to go to for the appropriate administration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Some questions were also raised on the PTIBs' fees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Their fees are based on the work done in a particular case and determined in line with market forces.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The fees, which are paid out from the bankruptcy estate, are ultimately approved by the creditors' committee or by the Court, if there is no prior approval by creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These mechanisms collectively work in tandem to introduce checks on PTIBs' fees to ensure that they are in line with market and that they are reasonable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The PTIBs' fees, additionally, may also be recovered from the bankrupts' contributions during the lifespan and the whole duration of the bankruptcy.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, you do not need to have had sufficient assets at the outset to meet the fees before the administration can start.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Along the way, there might be realisable assets that are called in, and this includes property acquired after a bankruptcy order as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, all that collectively comes out of the bankrupt estate and it goes towards the PTIBs' fees.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain asked whether the PTIBs' work might overlap with the work done by debt recovery firms or credit counselling firms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These firms take on the work pre-bankruptcy – so they might go and recover debts; they might go and issue demands, and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But once the bankruptcy takes place, that is when the PTIBs step in.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is on the making of the bankruptcy order by the Court that the PTIBs are appointed and their jurisdiction then begins.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There are various questions on the OA's role.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali and Mr Zhulkarnain, in particular, sought clarifications on the circumstances under which the OA is expected to administer the estate of the bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But let me just remind Members that this framework is designed to mandate the appointment of PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, the whole raison d'etre behind this is to ensure that cases are administered by the PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, when you asked about what happens when there is no such PTIB, or, in what cases can the OA step in, I would say as a starting point that it has got to be very narrow.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: That would be in line with the philosophy of this Bill – to keep it narrow so that parties go to the PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And it is only in the appropriate cases, like what I mentioned at the outset, for example, the public interest examples I cited earlier, or perhaps, given that the powers of investigation and prosecution do not devolve to the PTIBs – they remain with the OA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Perhaps in a case where you know from the outset very clearly that heavy investigation will be needed, or that there are likely to be prosecutions, in that case, perhaps it might be appropriate for the OA to take on that role from the start.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But really, those are examples: as I mentioned earlier, they are non-exhaustive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Because you got to look at the entire factual matrix, the particular circumstances of each case, to decide whether or not the OA should grant consent or should take on the role itself.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, as provided by statute, the OA will step in to administer the bankruptcy estate in the interim.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, in cases when an earlier appointment of a PTIB fails to take effect or the office becomes vacant after it has taken effect, then in such scenarios, the OA will step in.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The OA will step in and this question of consent or otherwise becomes irrelevant, because the statute mandates that the OA steps in so, that there is no disruption to the administration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Louis Ng and Mr Zhulkarnain asked how the Ministry will ensure effective oversight and quality of the PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: For example, the law confers powers of oversight over PTIBs on the OA, to whom creditors and bankrupts can also provide feedback on the conduct of the PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In particular, Members would also be aware that under IRDA, there are obligations to notify; there are obligations to submit a copy of the Statement of Affairs, to submit a report 30 days after the relevant anniversary of the administration date of the bankruptcy and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, this gives the OA the ability to look into the particular administration and for the PTIB to provide information to the OA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: PTIBs are also required to put up security which the OA can forfeit if the PTIB does not fulfil duties and responsibilities in accordance with statutory requirements.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Indeed, if there is dissatisfaction with the PTIBs' administration of the estate, the OA, as well as creditors or debtors, may apply to Court for various orders, including orders to modify the PTIB's acts or decisions, or indeed, in extreme cases, to also remove the PTIB.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In this regard, it is important to emphasise that PTIBs have incentives themselves to uphold; they are held to their own high professional standards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: PTIBs must either be accountants or lawyers and must comply with the professional standards of their respective professional bodies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Besides this, they must also pass various checks – including showing that they are fit, they remain fit and proper persons – to obtain their insolvency practitioners' licences.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Without these licences, as Members know, they cannot carry out bankruptcy administration and doing so without a licence is an offence.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In terms of ensuring that PTIBs are kept updated on applicable law and practice, the OA conducts regular dialogue sessions with PTIBs and will continue to do so after this expansion, to share best practices and developments in case law and practices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, MinLaw collaborates with Temasek Polytechnic on a biannual customised training programme on individual insolvency for PTIBs.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Ms Sylvia Lim asked whether there have been better experiences for creditors and debtors since the last bankruptcy amendment in 2016.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The bankruptcy experience, Sir, is generally an adversarial one, in the sense that the bankrupt would be looking to ensure that there is less or minimal monthly or annual pay-outs; the creditor wants to enforce, wants more share of the pie and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So that is a natural adversarial process, with creditors wanting to maximise recovery, debtors wanting to pay as little as possible.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In addition, undischarged bankrupts are also subject to various disabilities and restrictions.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The role of the PTIB, as with the OA before in administering these cases, is to strike a balance in the interests of both the bankrupt and the creditor, to ensure a fair and judicious outcome for both parties in the administration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not so much about whether it is a better experience or not, but whether it is a fairer one, whether we can strike a balance and the appropriate outcome for the creditors in all these cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain and Ms Sylvia Lim also asked if there have been complaints against the PTIBs' management of the bankruptcies.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Many of you might well have received complaints in the course of your regular Meet-the-People sessions where it is perhaps said: why is the OA asking for so much to be paid every month, because I only have a job that pays me this much and I have various dependants and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We have not found any of these complaints to be valid from a misconduct perspective.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Of course, to the extent that there are differing views as to what are the appropriate contributions, there might well be conflicts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But ultimately, as I said at the outset, I wish to assure Members that, ultimately, the Court – which appoints all trustees in bankruptcy – has the power to make orders in relation to the acts of the PTIBs to address genuine grievances and when the party seek redress, in the administration of bankruptcy estates.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In a context of a PTIB-administered bankruptcy, if there are instances where such offences might arise or where investigations are needed, then there is no change to the current position where the powers continue to vest with the OA who will carry out such investigations into the offences and make the appropriate prosecutions if any.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is what happens today by the way – the current position.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: On PTIB remuneration, Mr Zhulkarnain asked, in relation to the additional means of determining the PTIBs' remuneration, what safeguards to ensure that notices are appropriately given.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Notices are sent to the creditor's last known address, which is also used for other communication between PTIBs and creditors during bankruptcy administration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, typically, by the time it comes to remuneration, you will have gone some way down the administration, and that would have been the address, or the correspondence by which notices were given.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, it is unlikely that if you have been taking part in the previous administration, receiving part of the proceeds and so on, that it would not be also the appropriate address for remuneration notices.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Murali and Ms Sylvia Lim asked how the PTIBs' fees can be kept reasonable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would supplement what I said earlier by saying this that the OA does not regulate the fees per se of each particular administration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is left to the market forces in the manner I mentioned earlier and there are also parts of the legislation which ensure safeguards.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Naturally, creditors have a strong interest to ensure that fees are reasonable because, ultimately, the recovery and the fees come out of the same estate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But I thank Mr Murali and Mr Zhulkarnain for their suggestions on various things, such as prescribing that notices on remuneration may be sent by emails.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will study them when we prescribe mechanisms.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Next, on measures to protect individuals dealing with bankrupts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: This is an amount that will reasonably exclude most of the petty, lower-value transactions, which itself carries a lower risk signature.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you did set it too low, it would be too disruptive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Each time you take on a small amount, you have to make a disclosure.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you do not, then there will be an offence and that will be too prohibitive.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But that does not mean that should you collect other deposits and indeed enter into other transactions of a lower value.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: If you behave inappropriately, there could be sanctions by the OA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain also asked about information on employment history and status, and I thank him for those suggestions for a searchable bankruptcy database.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In accordance with our requirements, the OA allows, upon payment of a fee, inspection of this database for information on undischarged bankrupts, including PTIB details.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The OA is not statutorily empowered to retain or provide information on persons who have not been made bankrupts, but who are only facing bankruptcy applications.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Zhulkarnain understands why, because it might not come to fruition, that you will be made a bankrupt simply because you are facing a bankruptcy application.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, in these cases, for the OA to have to compile and maintain records of all individuals who are the subject of bankruptcy applications, so much more resources would have to be used.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It is not cost-efficient for us to do that.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I think Mr Zhulkarnain also asked about whether information collected by the trustee will be privileged.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Mr Zhulkarnain would know that, when a party is bankrupt, the trustee, who looks after the estate, owes a duty to all the creditors.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In other words, the bankrupt's estate is owned by the creditors in those cases.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And, in that situation, information about the estate should be made available to the creditors, so that they can then decide whether the distribution is sufficient, whether any claims, additional claims ought to be made and so on.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: But save for this, the trustees in bankruptcy, generally – and we will reiterate this message – keep information quite discreet and it is limited to this pool of people who need to know and who have an interest in the bankrupt's estate.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We regularly monitor the latest economic trends, engage our international counterparts, look at the lay of the land and get plugged in, into developments in this field, to ensure that our framework is kept relevant.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: And indeed, that is why ever so often, we come to this Chamber; to amend, to update the IRDA and other related legislation, to ensure that that we keep up to date.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In some cases, having done some market survey, the industry feedback has led to some of these proposals as well.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We will take on board the suggestions that various Members have raised and which we can consider as we implement the Bill.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: I would like to thank the Members for the support of the Bill, which will ensure better utilisation of public resources in bankruptcy administration.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: It will also support the PTIB industry and help the MSCs in the context of the SIP, and enhance protection of persons dealing with bankrupts in commercial transactions.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: This concerns the role of a PTIB in investigating the affairs of the bankrupt.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: I wonder whether, in these circumstances, whether PTIBs still have a role.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai
text: And, if so, how do we align the commercial interests of PTIBs with that of public interest?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: So, I think that broad architecture will align the interests of both the PTIB and the OA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: In the example that the Member cited, perhaps, that might be extreme cases where there will be some element that might interest the OA which might not result in or relate to recovery from the bankrupt's estate.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will resume the Chair at 5.45 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 5.21 pm until 5.45 pm.
